01 — Introduction

A designer by background.
A problem solver by nature.

I started with Industrial Design, learning how to turn ideas into physical products.

Over time, my questions became broader.

  • Q1Why do people behave this way?
  • Q2What problem are we actually solving?
  • Q3How should we decide what to build?
  • Q4What happens beyond the product itself?

These questions gradually led me from objects to experiences, from form to systems, and from designing solutions to understanding problems.

Today, I’m interested in the space between people, technology, products, and business.

02 — Method

How I approach problems

Not a process I follow because it looks correct. It’s the order in which I actually get from “something feels off here” to “this is what we should build.”

01

Observe

Look closely before jumping to solutions.

I start by understanding people, context, constraints, and what is actually happening.

02

Frame

A well-defined problem is often half the solution.

I try to separate symptoms from underlying needs and turn ambiguity into a clearer opportunity.

03

Explore

There is rarely only one answer.

I explore different directions, challenge assumptions, and use prototypes to learn quickly.

04

Decide

Design is also about making choices.

I balance user needs, business goals, technical constraints, feasibility, and experience.

05

Learn

Every solution creates a new question.

I reflect, iterate, and carry what I learn into the next problem.

Observe→Frame→Explore→Decide→Learn

AeroFlux

A purifier and wristband system for children with asthma.

Industrial Design · UX/UI · Healthcare · Collaborative 2024–25 →
← Work
AeroFlux

Designing a purifier that follows the child, not the room.

A mobile air purifier paired with a heart-rate-and-location wristband, designed to protect children with asthma without asking them to carry anything.

Industrial DesignUX/UIHealthcareCollaborative Project2024.09 — 2025.05

With 陳頎蓁 · Chang Gung University, Dept. of Industrial Design

01 — Context
  • — Among the highest rates in the world of asthma triggered by air pollution
  • — One of the most common chronic conditions in children
  • — Indoor pollution can run 5× higher than outdoors
  • — Poor air quality and over-exertion can both trigger an attack
02 — The Challenge

How might we protect a child with asthma through ordinary daily life and exercise, without asking a 6- to 12-year-old to carry, wear, or remember a purifier?

03 — Research

We started by mapping where existing purifiers actually fall short, then narrowed in on who this needed to work for.

6–12
Target age
The golden window for asthma treatment, cross-referenced against Piaget’s stage theory for how children this age respond to routine and self-care.

Existing purifiers, compared

Home Purifier
Cleaning power
Mobility
Desktop Purifier
Cleaning power
Mobility
Portable Purifier
Cleaning power
Mobility

None of the three solve the actual problem: a child moves through a home, and air pollution doesn’t wait for them to catch up.

Three needs, one product

01
Health monitoring suited to a chronic condition
02
Home air quality that follows daily movement
03
Emotional support, not clinical surveillance
04 — Design Concept

The concept pairs a mobile air purifier with a wristband that tracks location and heart rate.

01Wristband tracks location
02Signal sent to purifier
03Purifier follows & purifies
04Heart rate watched during activity
05Gentle reminder if too high
06Returns to dock to charge

Instead of one purifier per room, the purifier follows the child’s position from room to room. It also holds the temperature and humidity range known to reduce asthma triggers.

For heart rate, we used the standard exercise formula — (220 minus age) × 65–75% — weighted against the child’s typical weekly activity level, to calculate a personal safe ceiling. When the child’s heart rate nears that ceiling during play, the wristband warns the purifier.

Rather than reading as a clinical monitor, the purifier is shaped and animated like a small companion robot, so its reminders land as interaction, not alarm.

06 — Expression System

So the reminders would feel like interaction instead of a warning, we gave the purifier six expressions tied directly to the child’s state — it communicates before it ever needs to speak.

BRIGHT IDEA
Child starts following a prompt
JOYFUL
Daily activity goal reached
SWEATING
Nearing the calculated exertion range
LISTENING
Default, at-rest expression
WORRY
Nearing the danger threshold
SAD
Risk of triggering an attack
07 — A Day With AeroFlux

Walking through one full day was how the system actually got tested — not as separate features, but as a sequence a child and a parent would live through.

01

Wristband records activity all day while the child is out

↓
02

At home, a gentle nudge appears if today’s activity is still low

↓
03

AeroFlux tracks the child’s location indoors through the wristband

↓
04

Exercise mode switches on when the child is ready to move

↓
05

The purifier follows the child indoors, cleaning the air nearby

↓
06

AeroFlux reminds gently, in a calm voice, so the child stays reassured, not startled

↓
07

A voice reminder nudges the child to rest or reduce intensity

↓
08

If exertion or heart rate stays too high, the alert escalates

↓
09

Once the day’s activity is done, AeroFlux switches to sleep mode and returns to its base to recharge

Reflection

Designing for a chronic condition taught me that the harder problem wasn’t the air-cleaning technology. It was making constant monitoring feel like company, not surveillance. A wristband that only warns is stressful to wear. One that also plays is something a child will actually keep on.

Designing movement into everyday life.

A digital health promotion platform designed around Indigenous elders, movement, and motivation.

ResearchHealthcareInteractionProject Lead2024.07 — 2025.05
Fig. 02.0 — DANiTA key visual
Add image
01 — Context

For older adults, maintaining physical activity is not only a health issue.

It is also a question of motivation, accessibility, familiarity, and whether an activity feels meaningful enough to continue.

DANiTA explored how movement-based interaction could make exercise more engaging and personalized.

02 — The Challenge

How might we turn health assessment and exercise planning into an experience that feels encouraging rather than clinical?

03 — Research

The project connected:

  • User research
  • Elderly physical activity
  • SPPB assessment
  • Caregiver input
  • Disease history
  • Personalized exercise planning
  • Motion sensing
  • Dance interaction
04 — System
01Caregiver input
02Physical assessment
03Personalized plan
0410-stage dance experience
05Progress tracking
06Re-assessment
05 — Design Insight

Exercise does not have to feel like exercise.

For the target users, familiar movement, music, social context, and encouragement could become part of the motivation system.

Reflection

This project changed how I think about product design. The final product is not always an object. Sometimes the real product is a system of interactions, motivations, and behaviors.

Foldery

When saving becomes the problem.

A personal-taste product I defined end to end — from the observation to a complete PRD v0.1.

Product ThinkingPRD OwnershipCompetitive AnalysisUX2026.06 —
Fig. 01.0 — Foldery key visual
Add image
01 — The Observation

We save everything. Restaurants. Places. Products. Design references. Travel ideas.

But saving is frictionless. Remembering is not.

Over time, collections become overwhelming rather than useful.

02 — The Problem

How might we help people turn accumulated inspiration into meaningful understanding?

03 — Initial Assumption

At first, the product could simply organize saved content.

But that only solves the surface problem.

The deeper opportunity was:

Help users discover patterns in their own preferences.

04 — Product Direction
01Collection
02Organization
03Pattern Recognition
04Preference
05Self-understanding
05 — What I Defined

I owned the PRD end to end. Writing it was how I found out which parts of the idea were actually decisions and which were still assumptions.

  • Core problem and target users
  • A 7-step core flow
  • A three-tier feature priority table
  • Key data model decisions
  • Onboarding task order
  • Competitive analysis
  • Assumptions still to validate
  • Risk list
06 — Decisions & Trade-offs

The MVP validates one loop only:

01Import
02Sort
03Tag
04Remind

Two things were deliberately cut. A drag-and-drop canvas would have carried a high interaction cost for a behaviour I had not yet proven people wanted. Social features would have pulled review and compliance work into a v0.1, so they moved to v2.

One thing was deliberately kept early: the public / private field ships in the MVP. It costs little now, and it avoids restructuring the underlying data once sharing arrives.

07 — Positioning

I analysed six competitors, including Raindrop, mymind, Heptabase, and Plotline, and found the same gap in each: they all treat a saved item as a bookmark.

Foldery treats it as an unfinished task in someone’s life — a restaurant to visit, not a link to file.

08 — Why This Matters

The product is not only about managing information.

It is about helping people understand themselves through the things they choose.

Reflection

This project represents the direction I’m increasingly interested in: not only designing interfaces, but defining what the product should actually solve.

They come from questions, observations, experiments, mistakes, and conversations.

This is where I collect them.

Note 01 · Product

A good solution can still solve the wrong problem.

The hardest part of product design is sometimes resisting the urge to design.

Before asking how to solve something, I want to understand whether the problem itself is worth solving.

Note 02 · Design

What I learned from designing physical products.

Physical products taught me to respect constraints.

  • Materials have limits.
  • Manufacturing has limits.
  • Time has limits.
  • Users have limits.

Good ideas become meaningful when they survive those constraints.

Note 03 · Learning

Why I’m interested in Product Management.

I enjoy designing things.

But increasingly, I find myself more interested in the decisions before the design begins.

  • 01What should we build?
  • 02Why does it matter?
  • 03Who is it for?
  • 04What should we prioritize?
  • 05How do we know whether it worked?

That curiosity is leading me toward Product Management.
